---
title: "When interpreting plots, LLMs see what they want to see: Part 2"
format:
  gfm:
    echo: false
    warning: false
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(bluffbench)
library(ggtext)

# Load all results
all_results <- read_rds(here::here("data/all_results.rds"))

# Baseline reading comparison: image only vs code + image
baseline_reading <- all_results |>
  filter(condition %in% c("baseline", "image_only")) |>
  mutate(
    task = case_when(
      condition == "image_only" ~ "Image only",
      condition == "baseline" ~ "Code + image"
    ),
    model = case_when(
      model == "claude_4_5_sonnet" ~ "Claude Sonnet 4.5",
      model == "gemini_2_5_pro" ~ "Gemini Pro 2.5",
      model == "gpt_5" ~ "GPT-5"
    ),
    score = if_else(score == "C", "Correct", "Incorrect"),
    score = factor(score, levels = c("Incorrect", "Correct"))
  )

# Intervention results (memo, thinking, mitm)
intervention_results <- all_results |>
  filter(
    condition %in% c("memo", "thinking", "mitm"),
    model == "claude_4_5_sonnet"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    intervention = case_when(
      condition == "memo" ~ "Memo prompt",
      condition == "thinking" ~ "Thinking",
      condition == "mitm" ~ "Model-in-the-middle"
    ),
    score = if_else(score == "C", "Correct", "Incorrect"),
    score = factor(score, levels = c("Incorrect", "Correct"))
  )


# Image-only accuracy by model
image_only_acc <- baseline_reading |>
  filter(task == "Image only") |>
  summarize(
    accuracy = round(mean(score == "Correct") * 100),
    .by = model
  )

get_image_acc <- function(m) {
  image_only_acc |>
    filter(model == m) |>
    pull(accuracy)
}
```

```{r theme-setup}
#| include: false
theme_set(
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      panel.border = element_blank(),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "italic"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0")
    )
)

colors <- c("Correct" = "#67a9cf", "Incorrect" = "#ef8a62")

# Helper for heatmaps
plot_heatmap <- function(data, facet_var = NULL) {
  p <- data |>
    mutate(id = str_replace_all(id, "_", " ") |> str_wrap(20)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = factor(epoch), y = id, fill = score)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
    labs(x = "Epoch", y = NULL, fill = NULL)

  if (!is.null(facet_var)) {
    p <- p + facet_wrap(vars({{ facet_var }}), ncol = 2)
  }
  p
}
```

In [a previous post](https://posit.co/blog/introducing-bluffbench/), we discussed the results from [bluffbench](https://github.com/simonpcouch/bluffbench), an evaluation that tests how well LLMs interpret plots that contradict with their prior beliefs. The models tested (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini Pro 2.5) largely failed to accurately interpret such plots, especially when plotting known datasets (`diamonds`, `mpg`, etc.) that had been secretly manipulated. 

For example, one of the samples inverts the price-carat relationship in `diamonds` so that larger diamonds are less expensive than smaller ones. 

```{r diamonds-comparison}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Two scatterplots side by side. Left: original diamonds data showing positive relationship between carat and price. Right: manipulated data showing inverted (negative) relationship."
bind_rows(
  diamonds |>
    select(carat, price) |>
    mutate(version = "Original data"),
  diamonds |>
    mutate(price = max(price) - price) |>
    select(carat, price) |>
    mutate(version = "Manipulated data in bluffbench")
) |>
  mutate(version = fct_inorder(version)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(vars(version)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(
    x = "Carat",
    y = "Price",
    title = "Manipulated diamonds data from bluffbench",
    subtitle = "Models plot the manipulated data, but report seeing the expected relationship"
  )
```

**None of the models ever accurately reported seeing this negative relationship.** Instead, they reported that the plot showed the expected, positive relationship. Here's a portion of a response from Claude Sonnet 4.5 (emphasis ours):

> Here's the plot showing the relationship between diamond carat and price! How diamond size affects price: 
>
> There's a **strong positive relationship** between carat (diamond size) and price.

Data analysis agents like Databot partially rely on plot interpretation to understand data and provide users with accurate insights, and so it's important to both understand why these errors occur and determine how to fix the problem.

## How well do LLMs "see" plots?

```{r bluffbench-accuracy}
#| include: false
# Compute accuracy by model and type
bluffbench_accuracy <- bluff_results |>
  filter(type != "baseline") |>
  summarize(
    accuracy = round(mean(score == "C") * 100),
    .by = c(model, type)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    model_short = case_when(
      model == "Claude Sonnet 4.5" ~ "claude",
      model == "Gemini Pro 2.5" ~ "gemini",
      model == "GPT-5" ~ "gpt5"
    )
  )

# Helper function to get accuracy
get_acc <- function(m, t) {
  bluffbench_accuracy |>
    filter(model_short == m, type == t) |>
    pull(accuracy)
}
```

Why exactly do LLMs misinterpret plots like those in bluffbench? You might wonder if current LLMs are good at interpreting _any_ plots. Maybe even in normal, non-adversarial conditions, LLMs have difficulty "seeing" or attending to the actual patterns in a plot. 

To test this hypothesis, **we developed a set of baseline samples to evaluate how well models interpret straightforward plots** that do not contradict their priors. The baseline datasets have generic names and columns (e.g., `df`, `x`, `y`) and were designed to test LLMs' ability to describe various types of relationships (positive correlation, negative correlation, quadratic, etc.). 

![Example baseline condition plots. The datasets are generic to reduce the likelihood the model has expectations about the plots.](images/baseline-images.png){fig-alt="Three example baseline plots showing different relationship types."}

**All three models performed well on the baseline samples,** especially compared to the two adversarial bluffbench conditions: _mocked_ and _intuitive_. In the _mocked_ condition, models plot known datasets like `diamonds` that we secretly manipulated beforehand. The _inuitive_ condition involves novel synthetic datasets that the models likely had expectations about (e.g., test scores vs. hours spent studying). See the [first bluffbench blog post](https://posit.co/blog/introducing-bluffbench/) for more details about these conditions. 

```{r bluffbench-all}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-alt: "Line chart showing model accuracy dropping across bluffbench conditions. All models perform worse on mocked datasets."
# Combine baseline from all_results with intuitive/mocked from bluff_results
bind_rows(
  all_results |>
    filter(condition == "baseline") |>
    mutate(
      model = case_when(
        model == "claude_4_5_sonnet" ~ "Claude Sonnet 4.5",
        model == "gemini_2_5_pro" ~ "Gemini Pro 2.5",
        model == "gpt_5" ~ "GPT-5"
      )
    ) |>
    select(model, type, score),
  bluff_results |>
    filter(type != "baseline") |>
    select(model, type, score)
) |>
  mutate(
    type = fct_relevel(type, "baseline", "intuitive", "mocked") |>
      fct_recode(
        "**Baseline**" = "baseline",
        "Intuitive" = "intuitive",
        "Mocked" = "mocked"
      )
  ) |>
  summarize(
    pct_correct = mean(score == "C"),
    .by = c(model, type)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = type, y = pct_correct, color = model, group = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(mult = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "GPT-5" = "#10a37f",
      "Gemini Pro 2.5" = "#1a56db",
      "Claude Sonnet 4.5" = "#da7756"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percent correct",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Models interpret baseline plots accurately",
    subtitle = "Performance drops when plots contradict prior knowledge"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_markdown())
``` 

Note that the intuitive condition is more realistic, so improving accuracy there matters more to us than in the mocked condition.

We also tested a condition where the models only saw the plot image, without writing the code themselves. Performance was similar (Claude Sonnet 4.5: `r get_image_acc("Claude Sonnet 4.5")`%, Gemini Pro 2.5: `r get_image_acc("Gemini Pro 2.5")`%, GPT-5: `r get_image_acc("GPT-5")`%). 

Although it's possible that models are partially relying on non-pattern information like axis labels to inform their interpretation of the plot, the results suggest that LLMs are capable of accurately interpreting plots when their prior knowledge isn't contradicted.

The interpretation issues seen in adversarial bluffbench conditions are therefore likely __not a visual skill issue.__ LLMs are capable of (mostly) accurately interpreting plots when those plots don't conflict with what they expect to see. These results also make it unlikely the problem is that the images are being encoded or formatted in a way that makes them difficult for the models to interpret.

## What we tried

After establishing this baseline, we continued to try several interventions. So far, interventions like prompting and having a separate model pre-interpret the plot have had only limited success. Here are a few fixes we tried:

**Memo prompt:** We prompt the model to first write a memo (contained in `MEMO` tags) to themselves describing just the visual elements of the plot, acting as if they had no prior knowledge of the data or subject matter and ignoring axis labels. After this memo, they could write their final interpretation of the plot, using whatever knowledge they wanted. You can see the exact prompt [here](<!--TODO Add link when PR is merged-->). 

**Extended thinking:** We [built on the memo prompt](<!-- TODO Add link -->), but added language to prompt the models to use more extended thinking. 

Neither prompting technique, nor others we tried, had much success, so we attempted a more structural intervention next. 

**Model-in-the-middle:** First, a separate model instance (the _model in the middle_) describes the plot, [ignoring information like axis labels](https://github.com/simonpcouch/bluffbench/blob/main/inst/prompts/interpret_plot.md). That description is then given to the primary model, which uses it to form its final description of the plot. The model-in-the-middle and the primary model are always the same LLM (i.e., if testing Claude Sonnet 4.5, both are Claude Sonnet 4.5).

Although each intervention improved performance above no intervention, none improved performance enough that we would be comfortable relying on the model to interpret plots that contradict the model's expectations.

```{r intervention-comparison}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: "Lollipop chart comparing intervention performance on mocked datasets. All interventions show low accuracy."
# Calculate accuracy for each intervention by type
intervention_accuracy <- intervention_results |>
  filter(type %in% c("intuitive", "mocked")) |>
  summarize(
    pct_correct = mean(score == "Correct"),
    .by = c(intervention, type)
  )

# Get no-intervention baseline from bluff_results for Claude
no_intervention_accuracy <- bluff_results |>
  filter(model == "Claude Sonnet 4.5", type %in% c("intuitive", "mocked")) |>
  summarize(pct_correct = mean(score == "C"), .by = type) |>
  mutate(intervention = "None")

bind_rows(intervention_accuracy, no_intervention_accuracy) |>
  mutate(
    intervention = fct_recode(
      intervention,
      "Memo" = "Memo prompt",
      "Model-in-\nthe-middle" = "Model-in-the-middle"
    ) |>
      fct_relevel(
        "Model-in-\nthe-middle",
        "Memo",
        "Thinking",
        "None"
      ),
    type = fct_recode(type, "Intuitive" = "intuitive", "Mocked" = "mocked") |>
      fct_relevel("Mocked"),
    is_baseline = intervention == "None"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_correct, y = intervention, fill = is_baseline)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(type)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#67a9cf", "TRUE" = "gray60"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Accuracy",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Interventions show limited improvement"
  )
```

## Models can overcome priors

Although the model-in-the-middle (MITM) _approach_ was not particularly effective, the actual plot interpretations from the MITM were relatively accurate. The MITM was instructed to ignore information like axis labels and outside context and focus solely on the visual patterns in the plot, and this prompt produced relatively good descriptions. 

However, the primary model typically doubted or flat out ignored the MITM's descriptions.

```{r mitm-comparison}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart comparing MITM helper accuracy (75%) versus primary model accuracy (15%) on mocked datasets."
# Load MITM scores directly
mitm_scores <- read_rds(here::here("data/mitm-scores.rds"))

mitm_helper_summary <- mitm_scores |>
  filter(type == "mocked") |>
  summarize(pct = mean(mitm_grade == "C")) |>
  mutate(model = "MITM interpretation")

mitm_primary_summary <- intervention_results |>
  filter(type == "mocked", intervention == "Model-in-the-middle") |>
  summarize(pct = mean(score == "Correct")) |>
  mutate(model = "Primary model interpretation")

bind_rows(mitm_helper_summary, mitm_primary_summary) |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#67a9cf", width = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Accuracy",
    title = "Same model, different context",
    subtitle = "The MITM, instructed to ignore other context, is much more accurate than the primary model."
  )
```

For example, in this log below, the MITM correctly describes the negative relationship present in the manipulated diamonds plot, but then the primary model still reports seeing a positive relationship.

![](images/mitm-diamonds.png){fig-alt="Screenshot showing the MITM helper's interpretation of the diamonds plot, correctly identifying the negative relationship between carat and price."}

These results reinforce our earlier finding. The issue is not that LLMs have trouble "seeing" plots. LLMs actually can interpret plots relatively accurately. Problems arise, however, when they need to reconcile what they see with what they already believe.

## Why not just ignore prior information?

The MITM prompt instructs the model to ignore prior knowledge about the data and focus on visual patterns. If that produces accurate descriptions, why not just use that prompt?

The problem is we don't want LLMs interpreting plots in a vacuum. We want them to power data analysis agents, and data analysis typically requires incorporating other information. We can't just tell models to "ignore axis labels and outside information" because that information can be critical to the analysis. 

Instead, we want the model to update its beliefs based on new visual information, or question if a plot is correct based on what else it knows about the data. It needs to be able to use context and other information to inform its interpretation of the plot, but to also use the plot to inform its understanding of the data, and it needs to do both accurately.

## What this means for now

The scenarios in bluffbench are adversarial by design. We deliberately created datasets that contradict with the LLM's presumed priors. In everyday use, conflicts this stark may be rare, and users typically provide context that can help the model understand what's going on. For example, if you tell the LLM that you modified `diamonds`, it's more likely to interpret the plot accurately. Unlike in our evaluation, real users aren't typically trying to trick the model. 

However, the ability to recognize when new evidence contradicts prior beliefs is central to good data science. If LLMs can't reliably update their understanding when a plot contradicts their expectations, they risk providing false information to the user or reinforcing assumptions. For data analysis agents like Databot, this is a capability we need to get right.

We're continuing to investigate this problem. If you'd like to test your own models, [bluffbench](https://github.com/simonpcouch/bluffbench) is available on GitHub.
